title: Saying I Am Calm Fuels Panic, Yet Coaching By Your First Name Quiets It
description:
Experimental Chronicle — Ethan Kross (2014): Why Coaching Yourself by Your Own First Name ('You / [Name]') Quiets Panic Under Pressure, grounded in Ethan Kross, Emma Bruehlman-Senecal, Jiyoung Park, Aleah Burson et al. (2014) (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology). Empirical findings show that across 7 experiments in 2014 (JPSP), Ethan Kross and colleagues at Michigan / UC Berkeley asked volunteers to reflect silently on anxieties using EITHER first-person pronouns ('Why am I feeling this way?') OR non-first-person pronouns and their own name ('Why are you / [Own Name] feeling this way?').

At the circuit level, this episode examines how amygdala, prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that in the flagship acute-stress test (Studies 2 & 3), volunteers were given just 5 minutes to prepare an impromptu speech on why they were qualified for their dream job in front of stony-faced evaluators and a camera — using silent 'I' self-talk vs silent '[Own Name]' self-talk.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Ethan Kross, Emma Bruehlman-Senecal, Jiyoung Park, Aleah Burson et al. (2014). Self-talk as a regulatory mechanism: How you do it matters. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0035173
- Seth S. Leopold (2022). A Conversation with … Ethan Kross PhD, the Psychologist Who Knows What We Should Say When We Talk to Ourselves. Clinical Orthopaedics & Related Research. https://doi.org/10.1097/corr.0000000000002411
- Jason S. Moser, Adrienne Dougherty, Whitney I. Mattson, Benjamin Katz et al. (2017). Third-person self-talk facilitates emotion regulation without engaging cognitive control: Converging evidence from ERP and fMRI. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-04047-3
